lesson.title: A one-page cyber safety policy
lesson.subtitle: Rules your colleagues will read, follow and sign

video.title: A one-page cyber safety policy
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher and the school's cyber lead (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Salma opens a dusty cupboard in the head teacher's office and pulls out a thick folder. She blows dust off it and raises an eyebrow at the camera.
scenes.animation: Cupboard door swings open; dust puff; folder thumps onto the desk.
scenes.narration: Our school had a cyber safety policy. Twelve pages, in a folder, in the head teacher’s cupboard. Nobody had read it, and I’m the cyber lead!

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how to write a one-page cyber safety policy that your colleagues will actually read and follow.

scenes.visual: The twelve-page folder shrinks into a single sheet pinned to the staffroom wall. Four badges appear around it.
scenes.animation: Folder folds down into one page; badges pop in one by one.
scenes.narration: A policy only protects the school if people know what it says. So keep it to one page, in plain words, with a name next to every job. Review it once a year, and whenever something goes wrong.

scenes.visual: The single page fills the screen; five headings write themselves down it, each with a small icon.
scenes.animation: Each heading writes on as it is named.
scenes.narration: What goes on the page? Five short headings. Who leads: a named cyber lead and a deputy. Accounts: long passphrases, never shared, and two-step sign-in on email. Devices: screen locks, updates and approved apps. Data and groups: collect less, share with named people, back it up, and give every official group two admins. Incidents: report the same day, and nobody is blamed for reporting.

scenes.visual: Two columns. On the left an old poster of rules is crossed out; on the right a clean card with today's rules.
scenes.animation: Left column greys out as the right column fills in.
scenes.narration: Now, passwords: this is where old policies go wrong. Current guidance from NIST, the American standards body, says length beats symbols. At least fifteen characters when a password is used alone, or eight with two-step sign-in. No forced changes every month: change a password when there are signs it leaked. And check new passwords against lists of common and leaked ones.

scenes.visual: The staffroom wall with the school timetable. Teachers glance at it as they pass; a change is announced and everyone nods.
scenes.animation: Teachers walk past; a small megaphone pops when the change is announced.
scenes.narration: Think of the timetable on the staffroom wall. Everyone can see it, it fits on one sheet, and when it changes, everyone hears. Your policy should work the same way.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor at a staffroom table, pen in hand over a draft page. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Character slides in; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! I’m drafting the password rule for our policy. Which one should I write?

scenes.visual: The passphrase card gets a blue check badge. Beside it, two cards fade: a calendar with 'Password1, Password2…' and a single key shared by many hands.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the two wrong cards grey out.
scenes.on_screen_text: Long, and changed after a leak
scenes.narration: Long passphrases, changed only when there are signs of a leak. Forced monthly changes push people to add a one or an exclamation mark, and attackers know that trick. And a shared password can’t be traced, or taken back when someone leaves.

scenes.visual: Salma at a table with three colleagues, including the bursar with a ledger. Later, the page is read aloud at a staff meeting and everyone signs it.
scenes.animation: Steps tick off one by one.
scenes.narration: A policy written alone in an office stays in that office. Draft it with three or four colleagues, the bursar included. Read it aloud at a staff meeting and ask: is anything here impossible? Then everyone signs it, and new staff sign it in their first week.

scenes.visual: A classroom wall with five short pupil promises, then a parent reading a message in the official parents' group.
scenes.animation: Promises appear one by one; the parent nods.
scenes.narration: Pupils get their own version: five promises in simple words, on the classroom wall. Parents hear the parts that touch them, like which groups are official, and that the school never asks for money or codes by message.

scenes.visual: Salma holds up the twelve-page folder in one hand and the single page in the other. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A colleague says: “The longer our policy, the safer we are.” Agree or disagree?

scenes.visual: The 'disagree' card gets the check badge. Four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: Disagree: rules nobody reads protect nobody. Remember: one page, a name for every job, password rules from current guidance, written together and reviewed every year.

scenes.visual: Salma in the staffroom with a sheet of paper, asking three colleagues; she writes their answers down.
scenes.animation: Three speech bubbles pop; the sheet fills with three lines.
scenes.narration: Try it at school tomorrow: ask three colleagues for the one rule they would put first. Their answers are the start of your page.

checkpoints.prompt: Which password rule belongs in a modern school policy?

options.text: Change every password every 30 days, with a symbol
Long passphrases, changed only after signs of a leak
One shared staff password, so nobody gets locked out

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: length protects best, and forced changes only lead to small, guessable tweaks.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: monthly changes lead to guessable tweaks, and a shared password can’t be traced or taken back. Write long passphrases, changed after a leak.

checkpoints.prompt: A colleague says: “The longer our policy, the safer we are.” Agree or disagree?

options.text: Agree: more rules cover more risks
Disagree: people follow what they can read

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: one clear page that everyone has read protects more than twelve pages in a cupboard.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: rules nobody reads protect nobody. One clear page that everyone signs works better.
